name: multiple_dropdowns: The grocery.csv file contains pricing data on 40 different…
questionText: The grocery.csv file contains pricing data on 40 different products collected from 16 different Texas stores. Variables include in this data frame include: category: type of product (Cereal, Drink, Fruit, Snack, Spread/Sauce, Staple) city: store location (Austin, Fort Worth, Houston) income: average income in ZIP code where the store is located, in dollars population: population in ZIP code where the store is located price: cost of product, in dollars product: one of 40 grocery products appearing in various sample stores. (baseline category: "12 Pack DrPepper") type: type of store (Convenience, Grocery, High-end Grocery, Natural, Small Format) A prevalent social policy problem in many communities, "food deserts" describe urban, low-income areas that are under-served by grocery stores selling affordable quality fresh food. In a food desert, the best option for groceries might be a convenience store, rather than a full-service grocery store. If convenience stores charge more for the same product (perhaps due to lack of scale) under-privileged citizens might end up paying more for food than others living in more affluent areas. Do consumers in lower-income ZIP codes pay more or less for groceries? You decide to fit a regression model to investigate this phenomenon. To facilitate interpretation of the model, first add to the data frame a new column called income10k to record the income variable in units of ten-thousand (10000) dollars. Then, fit a model to predict price in terms of two predictors: (1) income10k and (2) product. Use large-sample inference to generate confidence intervals. Fill in each blank below with the best answer based on results of this model: The [ Select ] ["positive", "negative"] sign of the income10k coefficient suggests that consumers in lower-income ZIP codes pay [ Select ] ["more", "less"] on average for the same product. The 95% confidence interval for income10k suggests that (when comparing prices for the same product) an increase of $10000 is associated with a decrease of at most approximately [ Select ] ["1/2 cent", "3 cents", "2 cents", "1 cent"] in price. Because the confidence interval for income10k [ Select ] ["does not include zero", "includes zero"] we may conclude that this [ Select ] ["overall relationship", "partial relationship"] is [ Select ] ["not statistically significant", "statistically significant"] . This model estimates [ Select ] ["the same slope", "different slopes"] for the relationship between price and income10k across product categories.

blanks.label: The 95% confidence interval for income10k suggests that (when comparing prices for the same product) an increase of $10000 is associated with a decrease of at most approximately in price.
This model estimates for the relationship between price and income10k across product categories.

name: numerical: This question revisits the data on video-game reaction time…
questionText: This question revisits the data on video-game reaction time that we analyzed in class and in Lesson 14. Specifically, we'll consider three variables from this data set (two that we looked at before, and one that we didn't): PictureTarget.RT: the subject's reaction time in milliseconds when presented with a visual stimulus FarAway: a dummy variable for whether the stimulus (i.e. the “bad guy” popping up on the screen) was near (0) or far away (1) within the visual scene. SceneLetter: a letter code (b, c, d, e, or f) indicating which of five scenes the subject was presented with. (Note: the scene letters start at b; there is no scene a in this data set) Consider the following model and its corresponding regression table: lm(PictureTarget.RT ~ FarAway + SceneLetter + FarAway:SceneLetter, data=rxntime) %>% get_regression_table() %>% select(-std_error, - statistic, - p_value) Based on this regression table, what is the predicted reaction time for Scene b when the stimulus is not far away? Enter your answer rounded to the nearest millisecond.

name: multiple_choice: Imagine that you are a consulting data scientist for…
questionText: Imagine that you are a consulting data scientist for a candidate in the 2024 presidential election, working with data on political and economic metrics. You fit a linear model regressing presidential approval rates (percentage from Gallup polls) on the following predictors: cpi -- Consumer Price Index gasprice -- average gas price (dollars) sp500 -- S&P 500 index unemploy -- unemployment rate (percent) You use the model results to produce standardized estimates and intervals: Parameter | Std. Coef. | 95% CI ----------------------------------------- (Intercept) | 0.00000001 | [-0.11, 0.11] gasprice | -0.43 | [-0.72, -0.14] unemploy | 0.05 | [-0.13, 0.23] cpi | -0.40 | [-0.69, -0.11] sp500 | -0.06 | [-0.27, 0.15] Which of the following statements is accurate with respect to these model results? Holding constant other model predictors: (1) a 1% increase in unemployment is associated with an increase in approval rates of 0.05 standard deviations. (2) a one-standard deviation increase in the Consumer Price Index (cpi) is associated with a decrease in approval rates not exceeding 69%, with 95% confidence. (3) a one-standard-deviation increase in gas price is associated with a minimum decrease in approval rates of 0.14 standard deviations, with 95% confidence.

blanks.label: Randomization works, essentially, by flipping a coin independently for each subject in a study: heads, you get the treatment; tails, you get the control.

name: multiple_answers: Recall that "statistical uncertainty" is concerned with repeatability. Your…
questionText: Recall that "statistical uncertainty" is concerned with repeatability. Your results are "certain" if the results are repeatable (i.e., you observe little fluctuation in summary estimates) across different samples from the same random data-generating process.Which of the following is among the reasons that bootstrapping works as a practical tool for statistical inference? Select all accurate statements.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Resampling creates synthetic variability for our statistical summaries (i.e., sample estimates), helping us to quantify our uncertainty related to sampling variance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bootstrapping uses Monte Carlo simulation to approximate the variability that we would observe IF it were feasible to sample repeatedly from the same population.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the context of statistical inference, uncertainty arises from randomness inherent to our sampling procedure, not as a characteristic of any one particular sample generated by that procedure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Summary statistics (i.e., sample estimates) from different bootstrap samples will differ from one another—and theamountby which they differ from one another provides us a quantitative measure of our statistical uncertainty.
